extracted.intended_audience: improvisation students, teachers, workshop facilitators, and corporate groups learning improv
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and classroom games for teaching and practising theatrical improvisation—focusing on spontaneity, ‘‘yes, and’’ cooperation, attitude, exercises, and basic story-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play loudly, brightly and boldly
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform with visible joy, energy and delight; pronounce words with a big smile and exuberance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playing loudly and boldly raises the bar, gives permission to others, increases chances of success, and helps silence self-censoring. The teacher may demonstrate an exaggerated contrast (shy whisper vs lunatic bellow) to model the desired attitude. Encourage noisy, bright playing rather than meek or timid delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt an attitude of mild curiosity for idea generation
rubrics_metrics.description: When generating arbitrary ideas, use a mental attitude of mild curiosity rather than striving for a 'right' answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point at something, be curious about what word emerges; curiosity produces more ideas. This attitude is step one for training improvisers to generate arbitrary ideas on demand without stress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use positive cheerfulness to silence the internal censor
rubrics_metrics.description: A cheerful, delighted attitude temporarily quiets the internal mechanism that checks what you say before you say it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you act delighted, the censor thinks nothing needs checking, allowing freer, more surprising responses (example: saying a taboo word in a playful context causes no harm). This is a deliberate technique to lower inhibitions while improvising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage and normalize failure as part of learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Design exercises so mistakes are expected and learning-anxiety is managed; failure is instructive and essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Games should be hard/impossible to sustain so that mistakes occur and the class learns to cope. The 'What Are You Doing?' game demonstrates the importance of failure; groups that laugh when failing are progressing. Emphasize that the safety of controlled failure is preferable to fear of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train the ability to generate arbitrary ideas on demand
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop the skill to produce many arbitrary ideas quickly and without stress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularly return to simple games (Pointing At Things, etc.) so students learn when to produce arbitrary associations and when to generate connected ideas. This control over idea-mode (arbitrary vs connected) is crucial to success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use observation and debriefing to diagnose group tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe groups playing exercises and solicit feedback about what you saw—look for laughter, smiles, furrowed brows, tight shoulders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask groups what they observed after watching others. Use differences (serious/quiet vs happy/mistake-rich groups) to highlight how attitude affects performance. Tailor debrief to context: start with definitions (offer, block, accept) and discuss fun and momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish offers vs blocks; prefer acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat every new idea on stage as an 'offer' (to be accepted or blocked). In general, prefer accepting offers to build a cooperative world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptance allows two or more people to cooperate to construct a world and a story; blocking fights for control and prevents a story from starting. Introduce vocabulary (offer, block/deny, accept/yield/initiate) and emphasize acceptance especially with beginners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Say 'Yes' with enthusiasm (not grudgingly)
rubrics_metrics.description: When accepting an offer, respond in a way that genuinely inspires your partner, not merely a perfunctory or resentful acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The second version of the picnic game (grudging acceptance) is technically accepting but fails to inspire. Encourage enthusiastic 'yes' responses (body language, widened eyes, energy) because they motivate partners and build momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build chains with 'Yes, and' (connect each idea to the previous)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'Yes, and' to add a link that follows from your partner's last offer, creating a single chain of development rather than unrelated lists or parallel chains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The goal is to build on the immediate previous idea (e.g., Eiffel Tower → boat on the Seine connected to Eiffel Tower) rather than making a shopping-list of items all linked only to the first idea or jumping to new chains. Emphasize listening, visualization, and rapid confident 'yes, and' responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain energy, pace and loudness over premature quality judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep energy and momentum high; it's better to add another link with confidence than to stall analyzing whether the idea is 'good.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A feeble idea will often grow stronger as it is yes-anded. Encourage finishing the sentence quickly and keeping the pace rather than seeking a 'best' response. Corporate groups particularly need to experience this before they can play stress-free.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be good to work with—prioritize making your partner look good
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on being an encouraging, cooperative partner rather than on showcasing yourself; reassure and inspire your partner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat partners as if they are geniuses to make it easier for them to produce good ideas. 'Active listening' and visible approval (nodding, delighted responses) help create a productive onstage relationship. In other contexts (interviews, networking), aim to make the interaction pleasant for the other person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach blocking intentionally and sparingly (beginners: emphasize acceptance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that blocking can be a deliberate technique but beginners should be taught to accept rather than block; allow blocking instruction later after acceptance is established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct trivial blocks for novices (e.g., insisting on tea instead of coffee) but allow experienced performers to block playfully or for character choices. Use games like 'first to block loses' to sharpen understanding of what constitutes a block.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand narrative consequence of blocking vs accepting
rubrics_metrics.description: Blocking kills a promised situation and denies the audience what was suggested; acceptance develops and pushes the situation forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all 'no' responses are blocking (e.g., 'No' to a marriage proposal can create a story). Teach performers to assess whether a response kills an implied narrative promise or furthers it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate idea generation from evaluation in group contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: During brainstorming or early improvisation, gather many ideas without filtering; postpone editing/evaluation to a later stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the metaphor of filmmaking: get coverage (many shots/ideas) now and edit later. This helps pacify participants who habitually filter or deem themselves 'filters' and encourages quantity-first ideation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage playful, childlike rule-changing to maintain momentum
rubrics_metrics.description: Children will invent new rules and tap out joyfully; adults tend to cling to getting rules right and avoid playful improvisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mix groups and push for fast, furious play to break over-careful rule-following. Use exercises that invite inventing rules to keep the game moving and joyful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use posture/standing and physicality in games
rubrics_metrics.description: Games should be played standing (never sitting) and with expressive gesture to increase engagement and clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standing encourages the physicality necessary for improvisation and supports louder, more confident delivery and gestures; it helps in building chains and visualizing offers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story-building: create a PLATFORM, be obvious, avoid wimping, raise stakes, reincorporate ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: When teaching story improvisation, focus on gradually building a platform for the hero, making choices obvious, raising stakes, avoiding timid (wimpy) storytelling, and bringing earlier ideas back for structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'What Comes Next' game teaches these concepts and diagnoses weaknesses: a disconnected sequence is less story-like than a platformed progression. Use the game to train students to create coherent narrative progression and to reincorporate earlier elements for structure.
